solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Charlie (old-fashioned), near so-and-so, can, protecting Her Majesty

indicators.note: to protect something is to surround it, so one word wraps around the other

blocks.note: a vulgar term for an unpleasant person

explanation.surface: A list of oddments, as if describing some old-fashioned character called Charlie guarding the Queen.
explanation.walkthrough: Her Majesty goes inside the can after its first letter. A charlie was the old slang name for a watchman patrolling the streets at night.
explanation.definitionFit: Before police forces, the parish men who patrolled by night were nicknamed charlies, so the label old-fashioned marks this obsolete slang sense.

clue.text: Score vegetarian cutlet for Rev. Spooner? (7, two words)

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner famously swapped sounds between words, so the phrase is said his way

blocks.note: a nut chop is a meatless cutlet; swapping its two vowel sounds gives the phrase

explanation.surface: Someone orders a meatless cutlet for the famous tongue-twisting clergyman, and it seems to score.
explanation.walkthrough: Here the vowels, not the opening consonants, change places: nut chop becomes notch up.
explanation.definitionFit: To notch up a goal or point is to record or achieve it, the same as scoring it.

clue.text: It forms on scales of fish, number within reach

definitions.text: It forms on scales of fish

indicators.note: something within another sits inside it, so one piece goes into the middle of the other

blocks.note: to gain a place is to reach it

explanation.surface: A fish-biology fact about the glossy coat on scales, with a stray count tucked in.
explanation.walkthrough: Reach means gain, as in gaining the summit.
explanation.definitionFit: Ganoin is the hard enamel-like substance coating the shiny scales of certain primitive bony fishes such as gars.

clue.text: Star suspended? It involves these foot bones

indicators.note: the phrase involves, that is contains, the letters within its run

blocks.note: letters running across the two words

explanation.surface: A star hung up in the sky somehow connected with bones of the foot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It' points back to the phrase 'Star suspended', which carries the answer across its word break.
explanation.definitionFit: The tarsus is the cluster of seven bones forming the ankle and back of the human foot.

clue.text: Husband briefly in pen, making one feel very ashamed

indicators.note: one thing in another is placed inside it

explanation.surface: A man put in jail, a disgrace that leaves his family squirming.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pen' looks like a prison or enclosure; it is the verb to write.
explanation.definitionFit: To writhe is to squirm with acute embarrassment or shame, an emotional sense of twisting about.

clue.text: Italy treasure? Art style crafted with such old gold

indicators.note: something crafted is worked into shape, so these letters are rearranged
the answer is what must join the other phrase to make the whole, so the known phrase is taken away

explanation.surface: An Italian treasure whose artistic style was crafted with ancient gold.
explanation.walkthrough: A composite anagram: ART STYLE plus the answer can be rearranged to make ITALY TREASURE, so the answer is what is left over.
explanation.definitionFit: Aurei were the gold coins of ancient Rome, so as a plural noun the word means old gold money.

clue.text: Royal favourite to ponder losing 50% when king is buried?

indicators.note: losing half the word means only its first half is kept
something buried lies inside, so this letter goes into the middle

explanation.surface: Pondering what becomes of the Queen's favourite pet when the king is buried.
explanation.walkthrough: Half of COGITATE is COGI; R goes inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Queen Elizabeth II was famous for her many Pembroke Welsh corgis, making the breed the best-known royal pet dog.

clue.text: Distress keeps enveloping head

indicators.note: enveloping something means wrapping it round, so one word surrounds another

blocks.note: ras is a headland or cape

explanation.surface: Anguish that won't leave, wrapping itself round one's head.
explanation.walkthrough: A ras is a headland or cape, a word found mainly in place names like Ras Tanura.
explanation.definitionFit: To harass is to trouble or torment persistently, which is a verb sense of distress.

clue.text: Money always short in pool

blocks.note: M is the abbreviation for money
the poetic contraction e'er is a shortened ever, meaning always

explanation.surface: Someone forever low on funds while playing pool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pool' looks like the table game; it is a body of water.
explanation.definitionFit: Meer is an old spelling of mere, a lake or pool of standing water.

clue.text: Delicate in one's health

indicators.note: the letters are found in the words that follow

blocks.note: the letters across the word break

explanation.surface: Someone described as fragile in their general health.
explanation.definitionFit: Nesh is a dialect word from northern and midland England for someone soft, feeble or sensitive to cold.

clue.text: After pain and fever one's not available for dance

blocks.note: French mal, an ache, used in English in such words as malady

explanation.surface: After being ill with aches and a temperature, someone can't make it to the dance.
explanation.definitionFit: The malagueña is a Spanish folk dance and song from Málaga, similar to the fandango.

clue.text: Reverse of worthless American arachnid

indicators.note: the word that follows is read backwards

blocks.note: raca is a biblical term of contempt meaning worthless

explanation.surface: The opposite of a worthless American creature, as though one spider were valuable.
explanation.walkthrough: Raca is the contemptuous word in the Sermon on the Mount; only it is turned round, with the American added after.
explanation.definitionFit: Acarus is the genus of mites, which belong to the class of eight-legged arachnids with spiders and ticks.

clue.text: Eat nut stews, once on it for slimming?

indicators.note: to stew is to cook down and mix, so these letters are jumbled

blocks.note: an't is an archaic contraction of on it

explanation.surface: A dieter told to eat stewed nuts, with an old-fashioned remark about going on it to slim.
explanation.walkthrough: Once marks an archaic form.
explanation.definitionFit: An attenuant is something that thins or dilutes, so playfully it is a slimming aid, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Brown, small Australian shrew

explanation.surface: Describing a little brown shrew from Australia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Small' tells you to shorten Australian to its abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: The tana is a large tree shrew of Borneo and Sumatra, a squirrel-like insect-eating mammal.

clue.text: Decisions to do with being admitted into field of study?

indicators.note: being let into a place puts one piece inside the other

blocks.note: the arts as an academic area

explanation.surface: Rulings about admissions to a university faculty.
explanation.definitionFit: An arrêt is a judgment or decree of a court or sovereign, so the plural means formal decisions.

clue.text: Ghost, headless cleric, wanders here? Trick's involved!

definitions.text: Ghost, headless cleric, wanders here? Trick's involved!

indicators.note: removing the head of the word drops its opening letter
letters that wander move about out of their order

blocks.note: the word without its first letter
art is cunning or trickery, involved in the mix

explanation.surface: A spooky tale of a decapitated churchman haunting the abbey grounds, with some trickery afoot.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue paints the place: a headless monk's ghost would walk the quadrangle within a cloister.
explanation.definitionFit: A cloister-garth is the open court or garden enclosed by the covered walks of a monastic cloister.

clue.text: Poem created where Thai meets Kurdish

indicators.note: only the stretch where the two words touch is kept, so most of each word is cut away
meeting means joining up, so the kept end of one word runs straight into the start of the next

blocks.note: taken as written; its first letter is lost
taken as written; only its opening pair is kept

explanation.surface: A verse born of a meeting of two distant cultures.
explanation.walkthrough: The poem lies right at the junction, the end of one word running into the start of the other.
explanation.definitionFit: A haiku is a Japanese verse form of three lines with five, seven and five syllables.

clue.text: Paddy having a bit of an eye for a lady?

blocks.note: the iris is part of the eye

explanation.surface: An Irishman with a roving eye for women.
explanation.walkthrough: Paddy is a common nickname for an Irishman.
explanation.definitionFit: An Irisher is a colloquial term for an Irish person, as is the nickname Paddy.

clue.text: Work must follow joke about will being shortened – like a desk?

indicators.note: about here means around, so one word encloses the other
following means coming after, so this piece goes last

blocks.note: op, short for opus, a work

explanation.surface: An office worker told to sort out a joke will before settling at the desk.
explanation.walkthrough: Rot means nonsense, so a joke in the dismissive sense; op is short for opus.
explanation.definitionFit: A roll-top desk has a flexible slatted cover; the question mark admits other things may be roll-top too.

clue.text: What builds up in pipes with rust around? Lag required

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so one word goes inside the other

explanation.surface: A plumbing worry about rusty pipes that need insulating lagging.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lag' and 'pipes' suggest lagging; here lag is a verb, to hold back.
explanation.definitionFit: To retard is to delay or slow down, which is also what lag means as a verb.

clue.text: Month in which beast becomes frenzied

indicators.note: something frenzied is wildly disordered, so the letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: The time of year when an animal goes wild.
explanation.definitionFit: Sebat, or Shebat, is the fifth month of the Jewish civil calendar, falling around January and February.

clue.text: Embrace sailor, not quite a cut-throat maybe

indicators.note: not quite all of the word, so its final letter is dropped

blocks.note: a cut-throat is a straight razor

explanation.surface: Hugging a seaman who may well be a murderer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut-throat' suggests a killer; it is an open blade razor.
explanation.definitionFit: An abrazo is the Spanish word for a hug, used in English for the embrace given as a greeting.

clue.text: Japanese fish dish for influential expat in the East

blocks.note: tai is a Japanese sea bream
a pan is a shallow dish

explanation.surface: A Japanese fish dish served to a powerful foreigner in Asia.
explanation.definitionFit: A taipan was a powerful foreign businessman in China or Hong Kong, the head of a major trading house.

clue.text: You'll find this wacky clothing close to 'à la mode'

indicators.note: something wacky is crazy, so the letters are mixed up
clothing something covers it, so one piece wraps around the other

blocks.note: on can mean next to or close to

explanation.surface: Crazy clothes said to be the height of fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clothing' looks like a noun for garments; it is a verb, wrapping around.
explanation.definitionFit: Tonish means fashionable or stylish, from ton, high society, just as à la mode means in fashion.

clue.text: Cat is stunning in waders

blocks.note: to cat is slang for to vomit

explanation.surface: A cat looks stunning wearing fishing boots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cat' looks like a pet; it is the slang verb meaning to be sick, and 'waders' is not boots but birds.
explanation.definitionFit: Pukekos are New Zealand swamp hens, long-legged birds that wade in marshes.

clue.text: Old emperor or king having to demolish uprising

indicators.note: in a down entry rising reads from bottom to top

blocks.note: rase is a variant spelling of raze

explanation.surface: An old ruler forced to crush a rebellion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uprising' looks like a rebellion to put down; it is the instruction for reading the word backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Kesar is an obsolete form of kaiser, the title of emperor derived from Caesar.

clue.text: Dog (or deer) seen round north pole

indicators.note: seen around another letter means wrapping it

blocks.note: a stag is a male deer; Chambers also gives it for a male of other animals, as dog is

explanation.surface: An animal glimpsed circling the North Pole.
explanation.walkthrough: 'North pole' looks like the geographical spot; north is just a letter and pole the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Stang is a Scots and northern English word for a pole or wooden bar.

clue.text: Having entered university, loaf aimlessly, getting tangled up

indicators.note: aimless movement has no order, so the letters are scrambled
entering means going inside, so this letter goes into the mix

explanation.surface: A student drifting about at college and getting into a muddle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loaf' looks like idling, the verb; it is the word itself, rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: To run afoul of something is to become entangled or collide with it.

clue.text: Northern

blocks.note: the bare definition of the competition word
in a plain competition puzzle solvers write this clue themselves, so only a definition is printed

explanation.walkthrough: This was the competition word: Azed gives only a definition, and entrants submit their own cryptic clue for it.
explanation.definitionFit: Septentrional comes from Latin septentriones, the seven plough oxen of the Great Bear, so it means of the north.

clue.text: See tot pee in bog

blocks.note: to tot up is to sum

explanation.surface: Watching a toddler wee in the toilet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bog' looks like British slang for a toilet; here it is a marsh.
explanation.definitionFit: A sump is a marsh, swamp or pool of muddy water, the same as a bog.

clue.text: In India he carries messages, lot omitted by body of cyclists

indicators.note: what is omitted by a word is left out of it

blocks.note: the main pack of riders in a road race

explanation.surface: A cycling team that leaves someone out, with an Indian messenger thrown in.
explanation.definitionFit: In India a peon is a messenger, orderly or attendant in an office.

clue.text: A French female, when followed by English, showing apprehension

explanation.surface: A Frenchwoman, followed by an Englishman, looking nervous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Followed by' just places E after the other pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Unease is a feeling of anxiety or discomfort, close in sense to apprehension.

clue.text: Scottish venture yielding a fortune, sweet

explanation.surface: A Scottish business gamble that pays off handsomely.
explanation.walkthrough: The middle phrase is a third sense: a mint is a fortune.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scots mint is an attempt; a mint means a vast sum of money; a mint is also a peppermint sweet.

clue.text: Commonwealth regulars scan AZ clues

indicators.note: the letters are clued in a different order, so they need rearranging

explanation.surface: Veteran solvers of the Commonwealth regularly working through Azed's clues.
explanation.walkthrough: AZ is a nod to Azed himself.
explanation.definitionFit: Anzacs were soldiers of the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps, Commonwealth troops.

clue.text: Writer having pull at second joint, creating role of historical chief

explanation.surface: A writer pulling at a joint, as if in pain.
explanation.definitionFit: A pendragon was a supreme war leader of the ancient Britons, so this is the office of that leader.
